newsitem.title: USA: Soviet grain "raid" transformed U.S. farm sector.
newsitem.headline: Soviet grain "raid" transformed U.S. farm sector.

text.p: The wheat crop looked ragged and thin -- "the stands were terrible," Clarence Palmby recalls from a visit 25 years ago to the Soviet grainbelt -- but springtime was too early to judge the outcome.

Perhaps because of that, nothing came from an April 1972 sales trip by high-level U.S. officials. But soon after, the Soviet Union made one of the biggest grain orders in history -- acquiring $1 billion in U.S. crops in a frenzied six weeks.

Sometimes called the "great grain robbery" for the Soviets' speed and stealth, the sales of 25 summers ago were comparable to a world war or the Depression for their impact on U.S. agriculture, analysts and former government officials said in interviews with Reuters.
They cemented exports as the favoured path to U.S. farm prosperity and began the drive to free farmers from New Deal-era policies that limited output.
There were drawbacks too -- consumers rebelled at high food prices that followed the sales and esclating grain prices emboldened U.S. competitors to expand their output.
"It was a major breakthrough," said former Agriculture Secretary Earl Butz of the 1972 sale. Butz led the 1972 delegation accompanied by Palmby, then assistant secretary.
Butz urged U.S. farmers to plant "fence row to fence row" in the export boom that followed the sale.

The Soviet purchases were unexpected, given the Kremlin's preference for self-reliance, and breathtaking in size, totalling 18 million metric tons of wheat, feed grains and soybeans. Much of it was wheat, confounding expectations that feed grains, used in meat production, would top the list.

Moscow had purchased three million tons of U.S. feed grains in 1971 but Soviet officials were lukewarm when a long-term U.S. credit line was offered by Butz in April 1972. "It was a dull affair," Palmby said of the negotiations.
Butz and Palmby saw farmers reseeding fields in hopes of a recovery where autumn-sown wheat had failed. By late June, the Soviets could tell that drought was decimating the wheat crop.

A Soviet grain-buying delegation was sent to Washington, where it began bargaining with exporters and at the same time accepted a U.S. credit line that obligated the Soviet Union to buy $750 million in grain over three years.
By the time the White House announced the pact, on July 8, the Soviets quietly had bought 8.5 million metric tons of wheat and corn from Continental Grain Co.
"A surprise ... was the purchase of wheat and the quantity the Soviets wanted," recalled Bernard Steinweg, a senior Continental official who bargained with the Soviets.

Soviet grain-buyers were able to operate unnoticed because the Nixon administration had scrapped a requirement for export licenses for sales to Moscow. Rumours percolated in the grain market but there was little solid information until early August, when the Soviets began a second burst of purchases.
Nowadays, it is common wisdom that Soviet grainbuyers out-foxed the grain markets and got a bargain, further enhanced by U.S. export subsidies.
Prominent private consultant Willard Sparks said the 1972 sales profoundly altered U.S. agriculture.
"Until 1972, we were a (grain-) surplus country," Sparks said. "This really moved us to a market-oriented agriculture."

The euphoric surge in U.S. grain, oilseed and livestock prices soon angered cost-weary grocery shoppers. They also led other nations to grow more on their own or turn to other suppliers in the wake of U.S. export embargoes later in the decade when food shortages emptied grain bins globally.
The exuberant 1970s, when the average farm-gate price for the three major U.S. crops doubled, prompted farmers to over-extend in a spree of land and equipment purchases.
But sales and farm income withered in the mid-1980s in the face of inflation, high energy prices and a global grain glut.
"I think the Soviet sales, more than one single (other) thing" contributed to the run-up, said agricultural economist Bruce Gardner.

In contrast, the 1990s may mark the time when balance was regained after the gyrations of the 1970s and 1980s, analysts said. Rising incomes worldwide suggest broad-based and reliable growth in food demand. The long-term trend in global grain demand is clearly increasing, industry leaders say.
Participants in the 1972 sales say there probably will never be anything like it again. For one thing, exporters now must report any sizable sale of U.S. grain within 24 hours.
Moreover, crop information is more widely shared and there are few large-scale government buyers with a market like that of the now-dissolved Soviet Union.
